questions.q: createTask calls insertTask, which calls recordActivity. What problem does @zudojs/transactions solve here?
questions.explain: Passing tx through every function gets awkward as the app grows. The manager remembers the current transaction for you and decides what a transaction inside another one should do.
options: It makes each function run in its own separate transaction
It keeps track of the transaction in progress, so every function joins it without passing tx down by hand, and still works when called on its own
It replaces SQL with JavaScript objects
It makes the functions run in parallel

questions.q: Does @zudojs/transactions talk to PostgreSQL itself?
questions.explain: The package coordinates transactions but never sends SQL itself. The adapter turns begin, commit, rollback and the savepoint methods into commands for your database.
options: Yes, it has a built-in PostgreSQL driver
No: you give it an adapter that knows how to say BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK to your database
No, it only works with the in-memory adapter

questions.q: The adapter builds BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL … from a fixed table like { serializable: "SERIALIZABLE", … }. Why not write the caller's string straight into the SQL?
questions.explain: An isolation level is part of the SQL text, not a parameter. Looking it up in a fixed table means only the four known phrases can ever be sent.
options: Only values from the fixed table can reach the SQL text, so a caller cannot inject SQL through the option
Because PostgreSQL only accepts lower-case names

questions.q: Savepoint names go straight into SQL. Finish savepointName(name): return the name if it starts with a letter or _ and has only letters, digits and _; otherwise throw new TypeError(`Invalid savepoint name "${name}"`).
questions.explain: The regular expression /^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/ accepts a plain identifier only. ^ and $ make it check the whole name, so nothing can be added after it.
questions.expected:
SAVEPOINT sp_import_1
Invalid savepoint name "1abc"
Invalid savepoint name "sp; DROP TABLE tasks"
SAVEPOINT _ok

questions.q: Finish beginSql(options) like the lesson's adapter. Start with BEGIN. If options.isolation is set, add ISOLATION LEVEL and the phrase from LEVELS (throw TypeError("Unknown isolation level") if it is not in the table). If options.readOnly is true, add READ ONLY.
questions.explain: The SQL text only ever contains phrases from your own table. Object.hasOwn checks the key is really in the table (not something inherited like toString).
questions.expected:
BEGIN
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY
Unknown isolation level

questions.q: The in-memory adapter has no database, but the manager still sends its events. What does this print?
questions.explain: manager.run returns what your callback returns. The callback returned normally, so the manager committed: started, committing, committed.

questions.q: The callback throws. What does this print?
questions.explain: The manager rolls back and passes your error on unchanged, so you can still check its class. You never write a try/catch just to roll back.

questions.q: The second createTask breaks the UNIQUE rule on the title. What does this print?
questions.explain: The second call wrote its activity row first, then the task insert failed. The manager rolled back the whole transaction, so there is no lonely second activity row.

questions.q: How does a nested function know a transaction is already open, when nobody passed it one?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage is a value that follows the async work that started inside run, and is invisible everywhere else. A plain global would be shared by all requests at once.
options: It reads a global variable that holds the last transaction
The manager stores it in Node's AsyncLocalStorage, which follows your code through every await, timer and callback started inside run
It asks PostgreSQL whether a transaction is open
It looks at the call stack

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside the outer run, the default propagation "required" makes recordActivity join as a participant, even after a timer. Called on its own, the same function opens its own transaction as a root. Outside any run, getCurrent() is undefined.

questions.q: Three nested functions each call manager.run with the default propagation. How many COMMITs are sent?
questions.explain: The inner calls are participants: no second BEGIN, no own COMMIT. The root commits everything once, at the end.
options: One: only the scope that opened the transaction (the root) commits
Two: the first and the last

questions.q: A participant fails, and the root catches the error and carries on. What does this print?
questions.explain: The participant's failure spoiled the unit of work, so the transaction became rollback-only. Catching the error does not save it: the root's commit is refused with a TransactionRollbackOnlyError (a kind of TransactionRollbackError, so the instanceof check is true), and metadata.originalError holds the reason.
options:
caught it; rollback-only? true
true activity message too long

caught it; rollback-only? true
false activity message too long

caught it; rollback-only? false
true activity message too long

questions.q: Why does the manager refuse to commit after a participant failed, even when the root caught the error?
questions.explain: A participant has no way to undo only its own work in the shared transaction. If part of the work should be allowed to fail on its own, use a savepoint (propagation: "nested").
options: The failed part may have left half its work done; committing the rest would save an incomplete unit of work, so rolling back is the safe choice
Because the root is not allowed to use try/catch
To make the error message shorter

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tx.markRollbackOnly(reason) lets you do all the work and then throw it away: the commit is refused and the reason travels in metadata.originalError. The real import commits normally.
options:
thrown away: dry run
thrown away: dry run

questions.q: What is a savepoint?
questions.explain: Rolling back to a savepoint undoes only the work after it. The outer transaction stays healthy and can still commit.
options: A backup copy of the database
A bookmark inside a transaction: you can roll back to it, undoing only what happened after it, and keep the rest
A second transaction on another connection
A saved query you can run again later

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The default "required" joins as a participant. propagation: "nested" opens a savepoint inside the open transaction, so its callback gets a transaction of kind "savepoint".

questions.q: The table already has Buy milk, and titles are UNIQUE. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each title got its own savepoint. Buy milk failed, so only its savepoint was rolled back and the outer transaction went on. The two good titles were committed, giving 3 rows. Without savepoints, PostgreSQL would refuse every statement after the error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "mandatory" joins an open transaction and throws when there is none. It guards a function that must never write outside a transaction.

questions.q: A transaction is open. Which propagation rule pauses it and opens a separate one?
questions.explain: requires_new pauses the open transaction and opens a second one. That needs a second connection, so it only works with a pool, not with PGlite. nested uses a savepoint in the same transaction.

questions.q: What does propagation: "never" do?
questions.explain: "never" is the opposite of "mandatory": the code must not run inside a transaction. With none open, it simply runs without one.
options: It joins the open transaction but never writes
It throws if a transaction is open, and otherwise runs without one

questions.q: The code sends a "task created" email inside the transaction, and then the transaction rolls back. What went wrong, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: A database rollback cannot unsend an email. Anything that leaves your database (emails, messages, cache updates) must wait until the commit really happened.
options: Nothing: the email is rolled back too
The user got an email about a task that does not exist; send it in tx.afterCommit(...) instead
The email was sent twice; add a retry
The email was lost; send it in tx.afterRollback(...)

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: afterCommit callbacks run only after a successful commit and are thrown away on a rollback; afterRollback callbacks run only after a rollback. Both run before run returns (or throws) to your code.
options:
inserted Buy milk
email: Buy milk
inserted Buy milk
rolled back: Buy milk
failed

email: Buy milk
inserted Buy milk
inserted Buy milk
failed

inserted Buy milk
email: Buy milk
inserted Buy milk
email: Buy milk
failed

inserted Buy milk
email: Buy milk
rolled back: Buy milk
inserted Buy milk
failed

questions.q: Where in the callback should you register tx.afterRollback(...)?
questions.explain: When a line throws, the rest of the callback is skipped. Register hooks first, then do the work.
options: At the end, after all the work
Before the work that can fail; a line after the failing line never runs, so the callback would never be registered

questions.q: An after-commit callback fails. What does this print?
questions.explain: The data is already committed and nothing can undo that, so the manager does not throw at your caller. The failing callback did not stop the second one; the failures go to hooks.onError, where you log them or queue a retry.
options:
published task.created
onError: email service is down
task 1 saved

onError: email service is down
task 1 saved

questions.q: Build a tiny version of after-commit hooks. Finish createTx(): it returns an object with afterCommit(fn), afterRollback(fn) and finish(committed). finish(true) runs only the after-commit callbacks, in order; finish(false) runs only the after-rollback ones.
questions.explain: Keep two lists and run only one of them when the transaction ends. The email is sent only when the commit happened, which is the whole point of after-commit hooks.
questions.expected:
email sent
cache updated
log: rolled back

questions.q: Which errors are worth retrying the whole transaction for?
questions.explain: Serialization failures and deadlocks come from timing between transactions, so a new attempt usually works. Bad input fails the same way every time, and a duplicate stays a duplicate.
options: Every error, up to three times
A serialization failure (40001) or a deadlock (40P01), which mean "try again"
A validation error such as "title is required"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The simulated conflict (40001) was retried twice, and the third call committed. The validation error has no retryable code, so shouldRetry said no and it failed after one call.
options:
could not serialize access 2
title is required 1

questions.q: Finish shouldRetry(error): return true only when error.code is "40001" (serialization failure) or "40P01" (deadlock). It must also work for values without a code, including null.
questions.explain: error?.code is safe for null, and ?? "" gives a string that is never in the set. A unique violation (23505) is not retried: it would fail again.

questions.q: Finish delays(attempts, base): the list of pauses before each retry with exponential backoff. The first pause is base, and each next one is twice the one before.
questions.explain: Pause number i is base * 2 ** i. Waiting longer after each failure gives a busy database some breathing room.

questions.q: A transaction with retry sends an email inside its callback, and it commits on the third attempt. How many emails go out?
questions.explain: Retries replay the whole callback. Put side effects in afterCommit, which runs once, after the attempt that committed.
options: One, because only the committed attempt counts
Three: the database work is rolled back each time, but the email is not
None, emails are blocked inside transactions

questions.q: What does the timeout option of manager.run guarantee?
questions.explain: A timed-out transaction is never committed. To stop a slow query inside PostgreSQL itself, also set PostgreSQL's statement_timeout.
options: That PostgreSQL stops the slow query at once
That slow work is never committed: after the limit the transaction is rolled back and a TransactionTimeoutError is thrown
That the transaction is retried when it is slow
That the callback is given more time when the server is busy

questions.q: Why put a time limit on a transaction at all?
questions.explain: While a transaction is open, the rows it changed stay locked. Other transactions that need them wait, so one slow transaction can hold up many requests.
options: An open transaction holds locks that other requests wait for, so a long one slows everyone down
PostgreSQL closes transactions after one second anyway

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With readOnly: true the adapter sends BEGIN READ ONLY, and PostgreSQL itself refuses every write. That protects reports and exports from a bug that would change data.
options:
cannot execute DELETE in a read-only transaction
1

cannot execute DELETE in a read-only transaction
0

questions.q: This adapter only declares read_committed and no read-only support. What does this print?
questions.explain: The manager checks the adapter's capabilities before it sends anything: TransactionIsolationError for an isolation level it did not declare, TransactionCapabilityError for anything else, such as read-only.

questions.q: What is createInMemoryAdapter() for?
questions.explain: It is built into the package for tests and examples. It stores nothing, so it cannot roll back real data.
options: Tests and examples: an adapter with no database, so you can watch the manager's behaviour

questions.q: In a real server with a connection pool, why can't every query just use pg.query like the PGlite examples?
questions.explain: PGlite is one connection, so every query lands in the open transaction. With a pool, a query on a different connection would run outside it. The lesson reaches the transaction's own connection with manager.getCurrentHandle() (or getTransactionHandle(tx)) and sends the queries there.
options: Because pools do not support transactions
Each transaction's queries must go to the connection its begin() opened; another connection from the pool is outside the transaction
Because pools run each query in its own transaction

questions.q: What is the manager's onEvent option good for in a real app?
questions.explain: onEvent only observes: it tells you what happened, such as how many transactions roll back, without changing the outcome.
options: Changing the SQL the adapter sends
Receiving a lifecycle event for every step (started, committed, rolled back…) to send to your metrics or logs

questions.q: Finish countByType(events): count the events by their type and return a plain object, with the types in the order they first appear.
questions.explain: A Map keeps the order keys were first added; (counts.get(type) ?? 0) + 1 starts each type at 1. Object.fromEntries turns it into a plain object.

questions.q: Like the practice, completeTask throws a NotFoundError when no row was updated. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first call commits and its after-commit hook runs. For task 42, the manager rolls back and passes your NotFoundError through unchanged, so your API can still answer 404. The hook was never registered.
options:
notify: task 1 is done
NotFoundError 404 Task 42 not found

notify: task 1 is done
TransactionRollbackError 500 Task 42 not found

notify: task 1 is done
notify: task 42 is done
NotFoundError 404 Task 42 not found

questions.q: A participant function wants to "commit early" to make its row visible. What happens?
questions.explain: Commit and rollback are the root's job. If a piece of work really must commit on its own, it needs a separate transaction (requires_new, with a pool), or it should happen after commit.
options: It commits its own part of the transaction
It cannot: only the root commits or rolls back the shared transaction
It opens a savepoint and commits it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "never" runs without a transaction when none is open, and throws when one is. It is the opposite of "mandatory".

questions.q: Two requests run at the same time. Does each one see its own transaction?
questions.explain: AsyncLocalStorage keeps a separate value for each chain of async work. Both requests see their own transaction, even while they overlap. A shared global variable would mix them up.
